title: CRDT text editing (Yjs)
description: Yjs implements the YATA CRDT for shared text: every keystroke is an operation with a unique id, and replicas merge them deterministically regardless of arrival order. Google-Docs-style collaboration with no central server ordering — peers sync peer-to-peer and always converge to the same document.
method: Operations carry (clientID, clock); insert positions reference neighboring ops; merge is associative/commutative/idempotent; sync via state vectors and diffs.
usage: Use for rich-text collaboration; persist updates to a backend for durability; compact history periodically.

demo.code:
ops_a = [('ins', 0, 'Hello')]
ops_b = [('ins', 5, ' world')]
merged = 'Hello' + ' world'  # CRDT merge: both inserts survive, order deterministic
print('converged document:', repr(merged))

title: Conflict-free task boards
description: Kanban boards are natural CRDTs: cards as OR-Sets (add/remove with unique ids), columns as ordered lists, assignments as LWW registers. Two people dragging the same card concurrently resolve deterministically — last-writer-wins by timestamp, or multi-value for explicit conflict display.
method: Cards in OR-Set; position via fractional indexing; field updates as LWW-Registers with hybrid logical clocks; conflicts surfaced, never lost.
usage: Use fractional indexing for drag-order; show multi-value conflicts in the UI when they occur.

demo.code:
board = {'todo': ['card1'], 'doing': []}
# two users move card1 concurrently -> LWW by hybrid clock
board['todo'].remove('card1'); board['doing'].append('card1')
print('resolved board:', board)

title: Tombstone-free deletion (OR-Sets)
description: Naive CRDT deletion needs tombstones (remembering what was deleted) forever. Observed-Remove Sets avoid permanent tombstones: each add carries a unique tag, and remove only cancels observed tags — unobserved concurrent adds survive, and garbage collection can eventually drop old state safely.
method: Add = (element, unique tag); remove = cancel known tags; merge unions adds and cancels; GC drops fully-removed elements after causality is stable.
usage: Prefer OR-Sets for collaborative collections; run causal-stability GC to bound growth.

title: Hybrid logical clocks for causality
description: Wall clocks skew; logical clocks lose wall-time meaning. Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC) combine both: timestamps close to wall time that still respect causality (a message's HLC exceeds its sender's). LWW conflict resolution with HLC is deterministic and human-meaningful.
method: HLC = max(wall time, received+1, local+1); attach to every op; LWW picks max (hlc, node id) — causal and wall-clock-sensible.
usage: Use HLC for all op timestamps; break ties with node id for total determinism.

demo.code:
hlc_a, hlc_b = (100, 'nodeA'), (100, 'nodeB')
winner = max(hlc_a, hlc_b)
print('concurrent writes, HLC tie -> deterministic winner:', winner[1])

title: Delta-state synchronization
description: Shipping full CRDT state on every sync wastes bandwidth. Delta-state CRDTs send only what changed since the peer's last known state (tracked via version vectors), making sync proportional to activity, not document size — essential for large collaborative documents on mobile networks.
method: Track per-peer version vectors; compute delta = ops the peer hasn't seen; send deltas; merge; advance the vector.
usage: Implement version vectors per peer; fall back to full-state sync if vectors desynchronize.

demo.code:
vv = {'peerB': 12}
ops = [(i, f'op{i}') for i in range(15)]
delta = [op for i, op in ops if i >= vv['peerB']]
print(f'send delta: {len(delta)} ops (not all 15)')

title: Multi-value conflict display
description: Sometimes convergence shouldn't silently pick a winner: multi-value registers keep all concurrent values and show the conflict in the UI ('Ana wrote X, Ben wrote Y — pick one'). The data structure converges (same set everywhere); the humans resolve the semantics.
method: Concurrent writes accumulate in a set; UI renders all values with authors; user picks; the pick is a new write that supersedes.
usage: Use for fields where silent LWW would lose meaningful disagreement (names, decisions, priorities).

title: Fractional indexing for ordering
description: When collaborators reorder items concurrently, fractional indexing assigns each item a position key between its neighbors (a0, a1, a0V...) so inserts never renumber the whole list. Order merges deterministically across replicas — the trick behind Figma-like canvas ordering and collaborative lists.
method: Keys are variable-length strings ordered lexicographically; insert between neighbors by generating a midpoint key; rebalance rarely when keys grow long.
usage: Use for any collaboratively-ordered list; rebalance keys in the background when they get long.

demo.code:
keys = ['a0', 'a1']
mid = 'a0V'  # between a0 and a1
ordered = sorted(keys + [mid])
print('order after concurrent insert:', ordered)

title: Presence and cursor sharing
description: Seeing collaborators' cursors and selections (presence) is separate from document convergence: ephemeral state broadcast over the same sync channel. Presence uses last-writer-wins with heartbeats and expiry — stale cursors fade when a peer disconnects, no locks involved.
method: Broadcast (user, cursor, selection) on change; expire after heartbeat timeout; render remote cursors as decorations; never block editing on presence.
usage: Throttle presence broadcasts; expire aggressively; presence must never gate editing.
